analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $17 an hour over six years and ends subminimum wages for tipped, teen, and disabled workers.
analysis.headline: The Raise the Wage Act never got a vote: after being introduced on July 25, 2023 with 31 Democratic cosponsors, it was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and died there when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage in steps from $9.50 an hour to $17 an hour over six years, after which it would automatically rise with the growth in the national median hourly wage. It would also phase out the special lower minimums that let employers pay less than the full wage to tipped workers, to newly hired teenagers, and to workers with disabilities. The bill was sent to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum of $7.25 an hour, including millions of tipped restaurant workers whose employers can currently pay as little as $2.13 an hour in cash before tips, and workers with disabilities employed under special subminimum certificates.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage to $9.50 an hour on the bill's effective date, then to $11, $12.50, $14, $15.50, and $17 over the following five years.
After six years, the minimum would automatically increase each year by the same percentage as the growth in the median hourly wage of all U.S. employees, so it stops losing value to inflation.

Raises the base cash wage for tipped employees from the current $2.13 to $15 within five years, and then eliminates the separate tipped minimum entirely, requiring tipped workers to receive the full federal minimum plus any tips they keep — with an explicit right for employees to retain their tips.
Phases out the $4.25 youth subminimum wage for newly hired workers under 20 and repeals that provision of the Fair Labor Standards Act.

Phases out special subminimum wage certificates for workers with disabilities, raising their required wage from $5 an hour toward the full minimum over five years, barring any new certificates, and sunsetting the program.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who currently pay at or near the $7.25 federal minimum, especially restaurants, fast food, retail, and hospitality chains that rely on tipped and low-wage labor, through higher labor costs that may be passed to customers or absorbed in margins.

drawbacks.text: Restaurants and other low-wage employers would face substantially higher labor costs; the bill requires employers who may currently pay tipped staff $2.13 an hour in cash to reach $15 an hour within five years, a cost that would land on employers, customers through prices, or both.

The bill sets one national wage floor that rises toward $17 regardless of regional wage levels, so the required increase would be proportionally largest in lower-wage states and rural areas, where employers have the least room to absorb it.

Phasing out subminimum certificates for workers with disabilities ends a system some employers and families defended as preserving jobs, while the bill's own transition assistance only requires the Labor Department to provide information and referrals rather than guaranteed replacement employment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are large and direct: a near-doubling of the federal wage floor over six years, an end to subminimum pay for tipped, teen, and disabled workers, and inflation-proofing through automatic indexation. The costs fall on a concentrated set of low-wage employers, and the steepest adjustment is for restaurants in lower-wage regions. Critics' strongest objection — that the highest step, $17, exceeds what many small employers can absorb — is about the later stages of the schedule, not the initial $9.50. On balance this is a clear transfer from low-wage employers' margins to low-wage workers' paychecks.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on July 25, 2023 by Sen. Bernie Sanders with 30 Senate Democrats as original cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions that same day.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point afterward — the referral was the last entry before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
All 31 cosponsors were Senate Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay at or near the federal minimum — especially restaurants relying on the $2.13 tipped base wage and operators of subminimum certificate programs — kept the existing wage structure untouched because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with 30 Democratic original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on July 25, 2023 and never held a markup or reported it out.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 31 cosponsors were Senate Democrats and no Republican signed on; no vote ever occurred, so the chamber's full partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: The industry's tipped-wage model lets employers count customer tips toward the minimum wage, allowing cash wages as low as $2.13; the bill would raise that base to $15 within five years and then abolish the separate tipped minimum, transferring the cost from workers' tips to employers' payroll.

industries.industry: Retail, hospitality, and other low-wage employers
industries.note: Employers paying near the $7.25 federal floor would face mandated raises stepping up to $17 an hour plus automatic annual indexation to median wage growth, a direct cost to payrolls that employ the largest share of minimum-wage workers.

Organizations holding special certificates under Section 14(c) can pay workers with disabilities below the minimum wage; the bill would raise their required wage to the full minimum within five years, bar new certificates, and sunset the program, ending a pay structure these employers relied on.
